name: Ram
intro: Ram is an American truck and commercial-vehicle brand. You may hear older pickups called Dodge Ram, but current Ram branding, truck class, cab/bed configuration and equipment grade are separate ideas. Begin with 1500 versus 2500/3500, then the specific work a truck must do.
naming: 1500, 2500 and 3500 are truck-class/model names, not universal payload values in kilograms. Big Horn, Laramie, Rebel and other grades describe versions. A Tradesman name on one product does not identify every Ram’s engine or body.
warning: The course includes selected Canadian families plus explicitly labelled older/current road-recognition examples. Check the exact year, body, engine/drive configuration and current availability before using specifications or prices. Selected Canadian model families and clearly labelled recognition examples. Model year, exact version and availability must be checked before using a specification or price.

models.explanation: Ram 1500 is the brand’s light-duty full-size pickup family. Light-duty is a class description, not a statement that the truck has one fixed capacity.
models.tradeoff: Check cab/bed layout, actual payload and towing for the configuration. Passengers and accessories use load capacity; a premium trim does not create a universal tow rating.
models.compare: Compare Ram 1500 with matched F-150, Sierra 1500, Silverado 1500 and Tundra configurations for the actual job.
models.scenario: A friend assumes the number on the side tells them how much weight to load. Show why the vehicle’s actual labels and manual are needed.
models.power: Engines and hybrid-assistance systems have changed by year. A new or returning engine option does not describe every Ram 1500 on the street.

models.explanation: Ram 2500 is a heavier-duty pickup class than 1500. It exists for different load/use requirements, not simply as the 1500’s luxury equipment grade.
models.tradeoff: A more work-focused class can be unnecessary for ordinary use. Verify the actual load requirements, dimensions and running costs instead of buying the biggest class by default.
models.compare: Compare specific 2500 and 1500 configurations on the job and ratings. Diesel/gas choice and equipment also need matching.
models.scenario: A driver has no heavy-load requirement but likes the number. Explain what moving truck class is intended to change before discussing luxury options.
models.power: Gas and diesel engine choices depend on year/configuration. Diesel is a fuel/engine system, not a synonym for all heavy-duty trucks.

models.explanation: Ram 3500 is another heavy-duty pickup class, with configurations intended for different demanding load tasks. Single versus dual rear wheel is a configuration distinction, not a separate brand.
models.tradeoff: Use the exact vehicle’s load ratings and the actual loaded trailer requirements. More wheels or a larger model number alone cannot determine a safe loading plan.
models.compare: Compare matched heavy-duty configurations rather than a 3500 headline maximum with an unrelated 2500 base model.
models.scenario: A friend shows a dual-rear-wheel truck. You can recognize a configuration clue while still needing the model/year and load labels.
models.power: Engine, rear-wheel arrangement, axle and equipment affect capability. The family/class name is not enough to calculate payload or towing.

models.name: ProMaster
models.explanation: ProMaster is Ram’s commercial van family. A tall cargo van and a pickup solve different loading and access tasks, even if both can be used for work.
models.tradeoff: Check roof height, wheelbase, interior dimensions and the specific conversion. A camper or passenger conversion may change how the available load capacity is used.
models.compare: Compare ProMaster with exact Transit or other vans for the real cargo/interior task. A pickup’s open bed is not a substitute for an enclosed standing-height workspace.
models.memory: ProMaster = van, not a pickup trim
models.scenario: A friend wants a work van to carry tall equipment. Measure the inside and the doors, not only the vehicle’s outside height.
models.power: Powertrain and configuration are year/product-specific. Electric or other variants, where offered, require their own availability and charging checks.

workshops.title: Ram: classes, cab and bed
workshops.subtitle: Read a pickup listing before comparing its price.

pages.title: Class is not trim
pages.text: 1500, 2500 and 3500 are truck-class/model names. Laramie and other grades identify versions; those are different naming layers.
pages.example: A 2500 is not merely a 1500 with more screens and leather.
paragraphs: Truck class and equipment grade describe different choices.

pages.title: Cab and bed are practical dimensions
pages.text: A larger passenger cab and a particular bed length change both usefulness and total vehicle length. Know what you carry and where you park.
pages.example: Measure long tools and passengers rather than choosing from a side photograph alone.
paragraphs: Useful load space and parking fit are both physical requirements.

pages.title: Ratings are configuration-specific
pages.text: Engine, axle, wheel configuration, options and the actual load affect the relevant ratings. Do not substitute a range-wide advertisement maximum for the vehicle in front of you.
pages.example: Passengers/accessories use available load capacity, so the real job needs the actual vehicle documentation.
paragraphs: Configuration and actual loaded requirements matter more than a generic maximum.

pages.title: ProMaster is a different body job
pages.text: An enclosed commercial van and an open-bed pickup can serve different work needs. A camper conversion also has its own load implications.
pages.example: For tall indoor workspace, measure interior height and access doors, not just the exterior body.
paragraphs: A van’s usable interior and door openings determine whether the task fits.
